{"assignees":[],"author":{"id":"MDQ6VXNlcjgyNzQ1","is_bot":false,"login":"buremba","name":"Burak Emre Kabakcı"},"body":"## What

Two gaps in `client.notifications.send` (and the `notify` admin tool) block an interactive-card → in-app approval flow:

### 1. Cards with buttons never render in the web app

`notifications.send({ title, body, card })` accepts a `chat` CardElement (`section` + `actions` + `button` children), and the card **is** delivered with full interactivity to Slack/Telegram bot connections (`packages/server/src/notifications/service.ts` → `deliverToBotConnections`, `content = params.card ? { card } : { markdown }`). But the card is never persisted to the notification event and never reaches the web inbox:

- `createNotificationForUsers` (`service.ts:313`) inserts only `title`, `payload_text`, `metadata` — the `card` param is dropped from storage entirely.
- `listNotifications` (`service.ts:391`) selects no card field, and the activity feed (`manage_operations/activity-feed.ts:345`) carries only `title`/`body`.
- The frontend has no CardElement renderer on the inbox path — `attention-inbox.tsx` and `peek-pane-content.tsx` render title + markdown body only.

Reproduced live 2026-08-05: `client.notifications.send` with a sushi `section`+`actions`+`button` card wrote notification id `4820149`; the Lobu app shows the title/body but no buttons. Only a Slack/Telegram bot channel would have rendered the buttons.

### 2. `notifications.send` returns only `{ notified_count }` — no event id, no URL

The caller cannot answer "where did that notification land?" without a second round-trip:

- `handleSend` returns `{ notified_count: notification.created ? userIds.length : 0 }` (`tools/admin/notify.ts:203`).
- `createNotificationForUsers` discards the `INSERT ... RETURNING id` (`service.ts:347`) and returns only `{ created: boolean }`.
- The SDK signature is `Promise<{ notified_count: number }>` (`sandbox/namespaces/notifications.ts:61`), and `method-metadata.ts:507` documents the same.

So a reaction script must call `notifications.list` afterwards to learn the event id / notification id, and even then the row comes back with `resource_url: null` unless the caller explicitly passed `resource_url`.

## Why it matters

The intended loop is: agent sends an interactive card → human approves/rejects in the app → agent acts on the answer. Today the interactive part only works on bot channels, and the in-app row gives the agent no id or deep link back. Agents composing `notifications.send` cannot hand the human a URL, and the "buttons" half of the flow is a no-op in the product's own UI.

## Proposed fix

1. **`createNotificationForUsers`** — return the created `event_id` instead of discarding the `RETURNING id`.
2. **`notifications.send` / `notify`** — return `{ notified_count, event_id, notification_id, url }`, with `url` as `/{slug}/memory?content_ids={event_id}` (falling back to an explicit `resource_url` when provided). Update `method-metadata.ts` and the namespace type.
3. **Persist the card** in the event (`metadata.card`) and return it from `listNotifications` + the activity feed.
4. **Frontend** — small CardElement renderer for `button`/`link-button` in the attention inbox + peek pane so `notifications.send` cards are interactive in-app, not just on bot channels.

Note: `packages/server` and `packages/owletto` ship separately; step 4 is an Owletto pointer PR with `make ui-review`.

## Also surfaced (not yet scoped)

**1. `notifications.send` discoverability.** How do external agents driving `lobu` CLI learn this contract in the first place? The discoverable surface (`search_sdk` docs / method metadata) is thin here — worth deciding whether richer method docs (a `notifications.send` usage example with a card + the returned id/url) belong in `method-metadata.ts` or a skill.

**2. Community workspace onboarding is invisible to agents.** Members of the Lobu community (workspace at `community.lobu.ai`, org slug `lobu-cloud`) can join and get pinged by the shared hosted preview bots — Slack at `https://lobu.ai/slack` and Telegram at `https://t.me/lobuaibot` (`packages/server/src/preview/slack.ts` `PREVIEW_JOIN_DEFAULTS`, both platforms on the same Chat SDK adapter). The flow: join the community workspace → `/lobu link` (Slack) or `/link` (Telegram) a channel to your agent → `notifications.send` fans out to that bound channel via the shared `previewMode` connection (`resolveBoundChannelRows` branch B, gated to `preview_mode`).

But no agent-facing surface teaches this:
- `organizations.list` → `lobu-cloud` advertises `managed_auth` for GitHub/Gmail/Reddit/X/YouTube — **no Slack/Telegram entry** and no "join the community workspace and get pings" onboarding hint.
- `method-metadata.ts` `notifications.send` says it fans out to "the org's active bot connections (Slack/Telegram)" without explaining how a channel gets bound or that the shared community bot exists.
- The `lobu` skill says nothing about `community.lobu.ai`.

(The human-facing CLI onboarding is already complete: `lobu run` mints a claim and prints the join URL, the `/lobu link`/`/link` command, and — for Slack — the "add to your own workspace" option; `init.ts` points at the link-code flow. The gap is *agent-discoverable* knowledge only.)

So an agent has no way to learn *"join community.lobu.ai → `/lobu link`/`/link` a channel to the shared bot → `notifications.send` pings you there."* Candidates for wiring this: a `slack`/`telegram` entry + community-join hint in `lobu-cloud`'s `managed_auth` metadata; richer `method-metadata.ts` docs; or a "Community workspace" section in the `lobu` skill.

content.text:
Read the issue and verified every claim against `origin/main` (e1130c94c).

## Triage: valid, but the proposed fix mis-scopes step 4

**Claims 1–4 all confirmed:**

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| `card` dropped from storage | ✅ `notifications/service.ts:298` — the `metadata` JSON literal has no `card` key |
| `send` returns no id | ✅ `createNotificationForUsers` returns `{created: boolean}`; `RETURNING id` is consumed only for `notification_targets`. `notify.ts:203` returns `{notified_count}` |
| `listNotifications` + activity feed drop it | ✅ no card column in the SELECT; feed carries `title`/`body` only (real path is `tools/admin/manage_operations/activity-feed.ts:348`, not the one in the issue) |
| No frontend renderer | ✅ zero `CardElement` hits anywhere in `owletto/src` |

## The correction that changes the plan

A `chat` `ButtonElement` carries `actionId` — *"Unique action ID for callback routing"*. Server-side, `gateway/connections/interaction-bridge.ts:878` `registerActionHandlers` routes clicks against a **closed set of prefixes**: `run-approval:`, `tool:`, `suggestion:`, `question:`. Anything else falls straight off the end of the handler as a silent no-op.

So the issue's premise — "the card **is** delivered with full interactivity to Slack/Telegram" — holds for *rendering* only. An agent-authored button with its own `actionId` already does nothing when clicked on Slack/Telegram today. Shipping a web renderer without a dispatch path just puts dead buttons in a third place.

The actually-missing piece is a **callback receiver for agent-authored action ids** — that's new API surface and per AGENTS.md needs your sign-off before anyone builds it, not a "small CardElement renderer."

Second thing worth knowing: **the in-app approve/reject loop already exists**, just not for arbitrary cards. `action_approval_needed` notifications carry `interaction_type='approval'`, `approval_run_id`, and a server-side `interaction_inline` policy flag; `attention-inbox.tsx` renders real Approve/Reject wired to `useApproveRun`/`useRejectRun`. The cheaper design may be to let `notifications.send` mint a first-class interaction on that existing rail rather than invent a generic card-action bus.

## Suggested split

- **PR A** — return `event_id` + `url` from `send` (fix items 1–2). Purely additive: `service.ts`, `notify.ts`, `sandbox/namespaces/notifications.ts`, `sandbox/method-metadata.ts`. No design risk.
- **PR B** — persist `metadata.card`, return it from `listNotifications` + the activity feed. The `chat` package already exports `cardChildToFallbackText`, so the feed can degrade to text instead of dropping the card entirely.
- **PR C** — *design first*: extend the existing approval/interaction rail vs. a generic card-action callback. Renderer comes after this contract exists, not before.

Also fold into A/B: `method-metadata.ts:497` currently advertises the card as *"rich cross-platform rendering"* with no caveat — that line is what taught the agent to expect working buttons.

## "Also surfaced" status

- **#1 discoverability** — still open, and the overclaiming summary above is the concrete piece of it.
- **#2 community onboarding** — *partly closed* by #2531 (85a02464e). `skills/lobu/SKILL.md:61` now covers hosted-workspace join, `/lobu link`, and tells the agent to use `lobu run`'s printed URLs instead of constructing them. Still open: no `slack`/`telegram` entry in `lobu-cloud`'s `managed_auth`. I'd narrow this sub-item to just that, or close it.

---

**Confidence: high (~88)** on the code claims — read directly from `origin/main`, not the working tree. **Medium (~65)** on "a custom-actionId button click is a no-op on Slack" — that's read from the handler's control flow, I did not click a live card to confirm.

**Next actions:**
1. Post this as a comment on #2519 and retitle/split it into the A/B/C issues (say the word and I'll do it).
2. Ship PR A now — it's self-contained and unblocks the "where did it land" half without touching design.
3. Live-confirm the no-op: send a card with a custom `actionId` to the community Telegram bot and click it, to promote that finding to high confidence before anyone designs C.
4. Decide C's direction — reuse the approval/interaction rail vs. a new card-action event. That one's yours.

name: lobu
description: Set up new Lobu agents end to end and operate existing Lobu projects and memory: interview, scaffold, validate, authenticate, connect feeds, execute operations, and test Behaviors.
---

# Lobu

Use this skill when setting up a brand-new Lobu agent from scratch (follow "Onboarding a New Project" below) or when running, validating, evaluating, or connecting an existing Lobu project, or operating Lobu memory from a coding agent.

The `AGENTS.md` generated into a new project is the source of truth for the config API (the `define*` helpers, connectors, auth, Behaviors, memory) — this skill does not duplicate it. For an existing project, jump to "Core Model" + the relevant reference section below.

## Onboarding a New Project

Use this playbook when a new user asks you to build them a Lobu agent from scratch. Set it up end to end: ground yourself in what the user already has, interview, discover, scaffold, prove the complete local path, then offer the deployment choice. Do not call the setup complete until every path the user selected has actually passed end to end. If an external provider, authorization, deployment, or rate limit blocks the proof, name the exact blocker and leave the setup as blocked rather than claiming success.

### 1. Ground yourself in what the user already has

Before interviewing, look at what already exists so your questions and suggestions are personal rather than a blank slate. This is discovery, not a design decision — do not let it skip the interview.

- Local: run `lobu context list` to see existing contexts; check the current directory and home for existing Lobu projects (`lobu.config.ts`), configured MCP servers, and CLI auth state. Note what the user already set up.
- Cloud: if the user has an active session (do not create one just to look), call `client.organizations.list()`, `client.agents.list()` for each org, `client.catalog.listInstalled({ kinds: ["connectors"] })`, and `search_memory` for prior knowledge. This reveals existing agents, connectors, and memory you can build on.
- Tell the user what you are looking at so they can correct you, and let what you find shape the options you offer. Never treat this discovery as an identity signal: orgs, emails, or domains never prove a company or product, and never mention a competitor or third party unless it actually appears in what you found.

Do NOT ask for a login email during the interview. Email is only needed when a managed connector actually requires a session (step 3) or when the user chooses cloud deployment (step 6); ask for it at that point. Treat identity only as identity; never infer a company from an email address or domain.

### 2. Interview with concrete, personalized options

Interview the user one question at a time; wait for each answer, do not guess, and do not batch the questions. Anchor each question in what you found in step 1. Instead of asking "what agent do you want?" as a blank slate, summarize what you see and offer two or three concrete alternatives to choose from:

- "You already have org X with connectors A and B installed and N existing agents. Do you want to (a) add a new agent on top of those, (b) extend one of the existing agents, or (c) start something standalone?"
- "For what it should do, the common shapes are (a) a triage agent that reads incoming chat and files a ticket, (b) a scheduled report that summarizes new activity each morning, (c) a research agent that answers questions from your connected tools. Which fits, or what would you change?"

Offer a default so the user can answer "the first one" — decisive users and undecided users both move faster with a concrete menu.

- What company or product is this for?
- What does it do, and who does it serve?
- What is its public domain? (optional for a personal project)
- Do I have permission to research the public website and other public sources?
- What is the agent for?
- What should we call it?
- Who uses it: just me, my team, or each of my customers?
- How should it behave, and what may it do unattended versus only with approval?
- What should it remember? Model this as one to three entity types.
- Where does its data come from? Pick one connector or custom source to start.
- Where should people talk to it? Offer Web UI, API or SDK, MCP, Slack, Teams, WhatsApp, Discord, Google Chat, and Telegram without forcing a chat platform. If Slack is chosen, ask whether to join Lobu's hosted workspace for a quick start, install Lobu into an existing workspace, or use a custom Slack app; then ask whether to test the DM with Lobu, a named channel, or both, and whether people knowledge means conversation participants, bound-channel members, or the full workspace directory.
- Should anything run on a schedule?
- Which supported LLM provider credential does the user have?

If the user gave permission to research and has a public domain, research the company before proposing the design. Summarize its product, customers, workflows, and useful signals, and cite the public sources you used. Then propose one to three entity types, their relationships, the first data source, one or two useful Behaviors, and suitable interaction channels. Play back a short numbered plan and wait for confirmation before scaffolding anything.

### 3. Discover the surface before choosing how to scaffold

Check Node is 22-24 or 26+ (only Node 25 is unsupported), then run `lobu context list` and identify the named Lobu Cloud context; do not assume the active context still points to cloud after a local run. If a managed or cloud connector was chosen and there is no session, ask for the login email at that point, explain that Lobu will email an approval link, and run `lobu login --email <confirmed-address> --context <cloud-name>`. The person approving must sign in with that same email; knowing an address never grants access. After a successful login, an empty organization membership list is a tenancy/discovery result, not an authentication failure: call `client.organizations.list()` and explain the result. Never revoke or repeat login with `--force` unless the user separately approves that re-authentication.

Use ClientSDK through Lobu MCP or `lobu memory exec` with the explicit cloud context. Call `client.organizations.list()` to find public organizations offering managed connections. Call `client.catalog.listInstalled({ kinds: ["connectors"] })`; if the connector is not installed, call `client.catalog.listCatalog({ kinds: ["connectors"] })`. Inspect the selected entry's `detail.auth_schema`, `detail.options_schema`, `detail.feeds_schema`, and `detail.behavior_events` instead of guessing field names. If a matching live managed offer exists, explain it and call `client.connections.connectManaged` only after consent. Complete the returned user authorization, then run `lobu context use <cloud-name>` immediately before executing its `local_bootstrap_command` from the parent directory where the new project should be created; use `--here` only after entering an empty directory, and do not create a blank Lobu scaffold first. Ask for bring-your-own OAuth credentials only if no managed offer exists or the user prefers their own app.

### 4. Scaffold and build from the confirmed plan

If managed auth supplied a `local_bootstrap_command`, use the project it generated. Otherwise run `npx @lobu/cli@latest init` with the confirmed name and provider. Postgres is built in, so `lobu run` starts an embedded database; ask for `DATABASE_URL` only if the user chooses external Postgres. Read the generated `AGENTS.md` completely before editing `lobu.config.ts`. Use the canonical reference at `https://github.com/lobu-ai/lobu/blob/main/examples/lobu-crm/lobu.config.ts` when needed; do not assume that example exists in the new project's filesystem. Briefly explain how the chosen feed may use checkpoints to collect incrementally, emits events, builds shared entity memory, and gives both chat and Behaviors the same governed context.

`feeds_schema.<feed>.eventKinds` describes feed event semantics; it is not the list of Behavior event triggers. Use only `behavior_events` for an event-triggered Behavior. If the connector has no matching Behavior event, use a scheduled Behavior with a bounded named SQL source and read event text from `payload_text`. Validate the query against the running local schema before relying on it. If `feeds_schema` is empty, do not invent or trigger a feed; chat integrations such as Slack can deliver incoming messages directly. For Slack or Telegram, prefer `defineConnection` with `credentialMode: "hosted"` so no bot token is required; `lobu run` prints the exact hosted-workspace join URL, own-workspace install URL when available, and short-lived link command. Use those returned values instead of constructing URLs. A printed `/lobu link <code>` is one-time: redeem it in the first selected DM or channel. In an installed workspace whose installer is linked to Lobu, bind each additional surface with `/lobu link <agent-id>`; otherwise generate a fresh code for that surface. Mention Lobu in a channel test and verify the App Home separately. Lobu email login and Slack installation are separate: the email link authorizes Lobu CLI access, while an existing-workspace install requires the user or workspace admin to approve Slack's OAuth screen. Never describe Slack consent as an email approval. Use `credentialMode: "byo"` only if the user chooses their own app. Tell the user once which remaining secrets are required and add only `secret("ENV_NAME")` placeholders to config. Never open or request permission to read `.env`; inspect `.env.example` when present and declared secret placeholder names only. Never read, print, invent, or paste a real secret into source or chat.

If the user wants the agent to know people in Slack, ask whether that means conversation participants, members of bound channels, or the full workspace directory. Installing the app proves none of those by itself. Verify the selected scope by inspecting the people or member entities Lobu actually materialized and by asking the agent a roster question. If human-readable names or non-participants are unavailable, identify that exact product gap; never claim the complete workspace directory was synced.

### 5. Prove the complete local path

Change into the generated project directory and verify `pwd` contains the intended `lobu.config.ts`; never run project commands from its parent. Run `npx @lobu/cli@latest validate`, boot with `npx @lobu/cli@latest run`, and verify health and the local Web UI. With the embedded database default, `lobu run` creates and selects the local context and auto-applies the project; with an external `DATABASE_URL`, it does neither, so authenticate and apply to that runtime explicitly. Send a harmless direct chat message without tools.

Before consent to access provider data, inspect only catalog, connection, auth-profile, and feed metadata. For a `browser_session` profile only, `npx @lobu/cli@latest connector run <key> --auth-profile <browser-session-profile-slug> --check` resolves the device-bound path without execution. Never use `connector run` as a generic managed OAuth or env-profile check; those durable credentials stay at the gateway. Do not run a feed or connector dry-run before consent, because a dry-run may still read provider data. Ask explicitly before accessing real provider data. Only after approval, dry-run the connector or feed server-side and trigger the selected feed manually if that connector actually declares one. A feed dry-run records its run but persists no collected events, entities, attachments, checkpoint changes, or feed sync state. Run each Behavior once, poll `client.operations.getRun` with its returned `run_id`, and show each completed run plus any declared result event or entity. For a Canvas-only or reaction-only Behavior, do not invent a persisted output; use the Behavior `view_url` returned by Lobu. For Slack, treat DM, channel mention, App Home, and requested member discovery as four separate checks. Keep actions in approval mode unless the user explicitly approves execution. If any step fails, fix it and rerun that step; do not silently substitute a different path.

### 6. Offer the deployment choice

After the local proof, ask the user whether to keep running locally or deploy to Lobu Cloud. Explain that the embedded local runtime and Lobu Cloud are separate targets, and that keeping it local needs no further setup. Only if the user chooses cloud deployment, ask for the login email to identify the deployer, explain that Lobu will email an approval link, and run `lobu login --email <confirmed-address> --context <cloud-name>`; the person approving must sign in with that same email. Because `lobu apply` has no context flag, use `lobu context list` and then `lobu context use <cloud-name>` to select an explicit cloud context before deployment. Run `lobu apply --dry-run` first, show the target organization and exact plan, and wait for confirmation before applying. After apply, use only authoritative `view_url` values and link commands returned by Lobu; never construct URLs. Present the working access choices: Web UI, direct agent chat, API or SDK, MCP, and any channels the user selected.

## Core Model

- **Lobu** is the agent framework, runtime, deployment layer, and memory surface.
- Keep framework configuration in `lobu.config.ts` (TypeScript, `defineConfig` from `@lobu/cli/config`).
- Keep agent identity and behavior in `IDENTITY.md`, `SOUL.md`, and `USER.md`.
- Keep reusable capability bundles in `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` or `agents/<agent>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
- Use `lobu login` for CLI authentication. Do not use a separate memory login command.
- Use `lobu memory ...` for memory operations, MCP client wiring, seeding, direct tool calls, and browser-auth capture.

## Project Checklist

1. Read `lobu.config.ts` first.
2. Read the active agent files under `agents/<id>/`.
3. Check local skills under `skills/` and `agents/<id>/skills/`.
4. Use `lobu validate` after config changes.
5. Discover the live SDK and connector surface with `search_sdk`; never guess a method, connector key, feed key, connection id, or operation key.
6. When prompt or Behavior changes, run evals via promptfoo (see `examples/personal-finance/evals/promptfooconfig.yaml`). The in-house `lobu eval` command has been removed.

## Common Commands

```bash
npx @lobu/cli@latest init my-agent
npx @lobu/cli@latest run
npx @lobu/cli@latest validate
npx @lobu/cli@latest login
```

## Authentication

- Interactive (human at a terminal): `lobu login` runs the device-code flow with a browser approval.
- CI / your own automation: `LOBU_API_TOKEN`, or `lobu login --token <pat>`.
- Local `lobu run`: the CLI mints credentials automatically over loopback — no prompt.
- Headless, on a *user's* behalf: `lobu login --email <address>`. The server emails the user a one-click approval link and the CLI polls until they approve, then stores the scoped credential — no TTY, no pre-minted token. This is the auth.md "user_claimed" flow.

An external agent not using this CLI can drive the same flow over HTTP: read `<origin>/auth.md` (linked from the `agent_auth` block in `<origin>/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`) for the endpoints. Today only the email user_claimed flow exists (no zero-touch ID-JAG). Never fabricate a token.

<!-- lobu-memory-guidance:start -->
## Memory Defaults

Your long-term memory is powered by Lobu. Do NOT use local files (memory/, MEMORY.md) for memory.
- Lobu automatically recalls relevant memories when you receive a message.
- To save something, call save_memory with the content and an appropriate semantic_type.
- To search, call search_memory. Results include view_url links to the web interface.
- NEVER construct Lobu URLs yourself. When the user asks for a link, call search_memory to get the correct view_url.
- When the user says "remember this", save it to Lobu immediately.
- When a message changes a fact you already stored (an updated preference, status, count, location, or plan), first search_memory for the prior memory to get its id, then save_memory the new value with supersedes_event_id set to that id. This replaces the stale value so future recalls return the current one; the old value stays in history but is hidden from normal search.
<!-- lobu-memory-guidance:end -->

## Lobu Memory

Configure project-scoped memory in `lobu.config.ts` by setting the org on `defineConfig` and declaring the schema with the `define*` helpers:

```ts
import { defineConfig, defineEntityType } from "@lobu/cli/config";

const ticket = defineEntityType({
  key: "ticket",
  name: "Ticket",
  properties: {
    subject: {
      type: "string",
      "x-table-label": "Subject",
      "x-table-column": true,
    },
  },
});

export default defineConfig({
  org: "my-org",
  orgName: "My workspace",
  agents: [/* ... */],
  entities: [ticket],
});
```

Seed data records still live as YAML under `./data`. Then seed or operate the memory workspace with:

```bash
lobu login
lobu memory org set <org-slug>
lobu memory health --org <org-slug>
lobu memory seed --org <org-slug>
lobu memory run search_memory '{"query":"Acme"}' --org <org-slug>
```

Use `search_memory` first when the user asks about a specific entity or workspace memory. Use `save_memory` to persist durable memory. To update existing knowledge, search first, then save with `supersedes_event_id` so the old row is tombstoned rather than deleted.

## MCP Client Setup

Use the actual MCP URL for the user's runtime. Never hardcode a hosted URL unless the user explicitly asks for that instance.

Common setup commands:

```bash
# Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport http lobu <mcp-url>

# Codex
codex mcp add lobu --url <mcp-url>

# Gemini CLI
gemini mcp add --transport http lobu <mcp-url>

# Interactive client wiring wizard
lobu memory init --url <mcp-url>
```

For ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, Cursor, and other browser-managed clients, paste the MCP URL into the client's MCP/connector settings and complete OAuth in the browser.

## Browser-Authenticated Connectors

For connectors that need a real browser session, `browser-auth` launches a dedicated Chrome with remote debugging, stores its CDP endpoint on the auth profile, and the connector attaches over CDP at sync time (harvesting cookies live):

```bash
lobu memory browser-auth --connector <key> --auth-profile-slug <slug>
lobu memory browser-auth --connector <key> --auth-profile-slug <slug> --check
```

Use `--dedicated-profile` only when you want a non-default dedicated Chrome profile directory; use `--remote-debug-port` to customize the CDP port (default `9222`).

## Agent-Facing Tool Surface

The normal MCP surface is intentionally small. Flat administrative tools are not advertised to agents; compose through these tools instead:

- `search_memory` and `save_memory` for direct knowledge recall and persistence.
- `search_sdk` to discover current ClientSDK methods, signatures, connector feed keys, operations, access requirements, and examples. Pass `mode: "read"` when you only need methods safe for `query_sdk`.
- `query_sdk` for read-only TypeScript and `query_sql` for governed, paginated SQL reads.
- `run_sdk` for mutations and external operations. Use `lobu memory exec` from the CLI for the same ClientSDK scripting workflow.

Search before create to avoid duplicates. Prefer a read or dry run before mutations, never fabricate returned URLs or identifiers, and never delete from `events`; supersede or tombstone instead.

## Connectors, Feeds, and Operations

Connectors are the primary integration path for third-party services. Use this lifecycle:

1. Call `search_sdk` with the service name. It returns installed and installable connectors, declared feed keys, SDK methods, and readiness details.
2. Use `query_sdk` to inspect `client.catalog.listInstalled({ kinds: ["connectors"] })`, `client.catalog.listCatalog({ kinds: ["connectors"] })`, and `client.connections.list()` when you need a complete inventory.
3. In `run_sdk`, call `client.connections.connect({ connector_key })`. An `active` or `pending_auth` result carries a `connection_id`. A `setup_required` result is a continuation: follow its `next_action`, `resume_call`, or `completion_check` exactly and do not create a feed until a `connection_id` is present. If the result carries `self_install_url` (a Slack app bootstrap deep link), offer it to the user so they can create + install their own app and paste back the bot token / signing secret.
4. Create the feed with `client.feeds.create({ connection_id, feed_key, config })`. Connecting alone collects nothing.
5. Trigger and verify it with `client.feeds.trigger({ feed_id, dry_run: true })`, then inspect `client.feeds.get({ feed_id })`. A dry run prevents Lobu writes but cannot undo upstream side effects caused by the connector.

Virtual feeds query the provider live and can be read with `client.feeds.readMany(...)`; collected feeds persist events for search and relational queries.

Discover executable connector actions with `client.operations.listAvailable({ query, include_disconnected: true })`. Use the returned connection and operation target with `client.operations.execute({ connection_id, operation_key, input })`. If readiness is disconnected, follow the returned next action instead of guessing a connection. Approval-gated execution returns `pending_approval`; surface that state rather than treating it as failure.

## Data Ingestion

- Use `lobu memory seed` for small declarative YAML datasets under `./data`; it processes records sequentially and is not a bulk-backfill path.
- Use `client.knowledge.save` for schema-less semantic history such as messages, notes, observations, and content. Pass `supersedes_event_id` when replacing an existing fact.
- Use `client.entities.create` / `client.entities.update` only for strict structured records that match declared entity schemas.
- For large backfills, send bounded chunks through `run_sdk` / `lobu memory exec` and use `Promise.allSettled` so conflicts and partial failures remain visible.

```ts
export default async (_ctx, client) => {
  const records = [
    { content: "...", semantic_type: "note" },
    { content: "...", semantic_type: "observation" },
  ];
  return Promise.allSettled(records.map((record) => client.knowledge.save(record)));
};
```

content.text:
I traced the whole surface. The short version: **the loop the issue asks for already exists and works in production — `notifications.send` is the one door onto it with the wiring cut.** So the proper fix is subtraction plus one registry entry, not a new card system.

## What's actually there

`notifications/triggers.ts:363` `buildActionApprovalCard` already builds a `chat` Card with `Actions([Button("run-approval:<runId>:approve"), Button(…reject), LinkButton(url)])`, passes it as the **same `card` param** to `createNotificationForUsers`, fans it to bound Slack/Telegram channels, and the clicks land at `interaction-bridge.ts:901` → `manage_operations approve/reject`. The same notification hits the in-app inbox, where `listNotifications` (service.ts:411-420) joins the pending approval and `attention-inbox.tsx` renders live Approve/Reject.

Behind it sits one genuinely good durable primitive:

- `runs.approval_status` + `events.interaction_{type,status,input_schema,input,output,error}` + `supersedes_event_id`
- `BuilderApprovalHandler[]` (manage_operations.ts:1814) — commented *"Add a new builder family by registering another handler here"*
- human-only decisions (`requireHumanApprovalContext`: agents literally cannot approve), admin-or-owner authority, reviewer stamped down the whole chain
- 7-day expiry (`expire-pending-approvals.ts`) covering `run_type IN ('action','internal')` generically
- `ApproveAction.input` already carries structured human input, already validated against `interaction_input_schema`
- and `event-card.tsx:1192-1460` already renders that schema as a **form**, plus input/output/error/reviewer

So: durable state ✅, human gate ✅, expiry ✅, audit ✅, chat buttons ✅, web buttons ✅, structured answer ✅, form UI ✅.

## The actual defect

`notifications.send` was given a **raw `card` passthrough instead of a handle on that rail**. A caller-authored card is unroutable (no handler prefix → `registerActionHandlers` silently no-ops), unpersisted (dropped at service.ts:313), stateless (no pending row to expire/authorize/audit), and unanswerable (no `interaction_output`).

**The `card` parameter is the bug.** Adding a web renderer plus a callback bus would build a second interaction system beside the one that works — new routing, new pending store, new expiry, new authz, and the agent still polling. That's the gap-generator, so the plan deletes that path rather than extending it.

## Plan

**P0 — return identity.** `createNotificationForUsers` returns `{created, eventId}`; `handleSend` returns `{notified_count, event_id, url}`. `url` = `buildResourcePermalink(orgSlug, {kind:'event', eventId})`, or `resource_url` when given. One id, not two — `markAsRead` keys on `events.id`, so `notification_id === event_id`; saying otherwise in the contract would invent a distinction. Contract edit ⇒ the client-regen CI gate fires.

**P0b — persist the card, reject the lying half.** Store `metadata.card`, return it from `listNotifications` + the activity feed (`cardChildToFallbackText` gives the feed a text degrade instead of a drop). At the `notifications.send` boundary, **reject `actions`/`button` children with a caller-authored `actionId`**, pointing the error at the interaction param. `link-button` stays — it's a URL and works everywhere. This closes the dead-button class at the door instead of spreading it to a third surface.

**P1 — one primitive for "ask a human"** (the piece that doesn't exist). Mint a pending `run_type='internal'` run under a new `action_key`, plus a pending `interaction_type='approval'` event carrying the agent's `interaction_input_schema`, then send the notification as `type='action_approval_needed'` with `resourceType='event'` / `resourceId=<proposal event id>` and a **server-built** card. Register one `BuilderApprovalHandler` whose `apply()` records the human's `input` into `interaction_output` and performs no side effect. Everything above comes free.

The one vocabulary cost: buttons say Approve/Reject. `BuilderApprovalHandler` already has `nounLabel`; adding a family-supplied label pair lets the card say Confirm/Decline or the agent's own words — small addition, no new mechanism.

**P2 — the agent acts on the answer.** `client.operations.getRun(run_id)` already returns status + output: zero new mechanism, fine for scheduled Behaviors. Event-driven resume would want a platform Behavior event, and **there's a real blocker I won't paper over**: `platform-events.ts` builds a `ConnectorTriggerSignal` requiring `connector_key` + non-null `connection_id` and returns early when it's null. An interaction has neither. That needs a connection-less platform-signal variant decided first.

**P3 — frontend consolidation** (Owletto pointer PR, `make ui-review` + human `/ui-approve`). No CardElement renderer. Extract the events-tab interaction card into a shared component and use it in `attention-inbox.tsx` and `peek-pane-content.tsx`, deleting the inbox's partial reimplementation. Every surface gains the form and the output.

**P4 — docs.** Correct `method-metadata.ts:497`'s "rich cross-platform rendering" claim (it's what taught the agent to expect working buttons), document `event_id`/`url` and the interaction param with a full ask→approve→read example. Narrow the community-workspace item to the missing `lobu-cloud` `managed_auth` slack/telegram entry — #2531 already shipped the join + `/lobu link` playbook.

**Net new mechanism: one handler registry entry.** No new table, endpoint, callback prefix, expiry job, or authz path. Two things get deleted: the unroutable card-button path and the inbox's duplicate card.

## One decision is yours

P1 adds SDK surface, which AGENTS.md says I don't do unasked.

-- Widen the events interaction CHECK constraints to admit the non-blocking
-- "suggested actions" interaction type. Suggestions are agent-emitted chips
-- the user MAY tap to send a message as a new turn.
-- They are a first-class interaction type on the same durable-event substrate
-- as `approval` cards (persisted, replayed on reload, superseded each turn),
-- but non-blocking: they are never resolved by a click. A later successful
-- turn supersedes or clears them, so their live status is 'current' rather
-- than the approval lifecycle 'pending' -> approved/rejected.
--
-- Replace each constraint atomically, then validate it separately. Adding the
-- replacement as NOT VALID avoids scanning events while holding the
-- ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock needed by ALTER TABLE; VALIDATE performs the scan
-- under a weaker lock. Existing rows already satisfy the wider predicates.
-- Safe under a rolling deploy: old pods only write the pre-existing values,
-- which remain legal.

-- interaction_type: allow 'suggestion' alongside 'none' | 'approval'.
ALTER TABLE public.events
  DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS events_interaction_type_check,
  ADD CONSTRAINT events_interaction_type_check CHECK (
    interaction_type = ANY (ARRAY[
      'none'::text, 'approval'::text, 'suggestion'::text
    ])
  ) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE public.events
  VALIDATE CONSTRAINT events_interaction_type_check;

-- interaction_status: allow 'current' (the live-suggestion marker) alongside
-- the approval lifecycle statuses.
ALTER TABLE public.events
  DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS events_interaction_status_check,
  ADD CONSTRAINT events_interaction_status_check CHECK (
    interaction_status = ANY (ARRAY[
      'pending'::text, 'approved'::text, 'rejected'::text,
      'completed'::text, 'failed'::text, 'current'::text
    ])
  ) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE public.events
  VALIDATE CONSTRAINT events_interaction_status_check;

-- API/Builder conversations have no numeric connection_id, so the existing
-- (connection_id, origin_id) index cannot serve suggestion lookups.
--
-- Deliberately NO interaction_status filter in the predicate:
-- persistSuggestion's prior-row lookup is status-agnostic (it must chain past
-- 'completed' clear markers), so a status='current' predicate would exclude
-- exactly the rows that hot path reads and degrade it to an org-wide scan
-- under the suggestion advisory lock. Status-filtered readers still use this
-- index with status as a post-filter.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_events_live_suggestion_origin
  ON public.events (organization_id, origin_id)
  WHERE superseded_by IS NULL
    AND interaction_type = 'suggestion';

-- migrate:down transaction:false

-- Refuse to narrow the constraints while suggestion rows remain. The check
-- and both replacements run in one transaction so a failed rollback leaves
-- the wider constraints intact.
DO $$
BEGIN
  IF EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM public.events
    WHERE interaction_type = 'suggestion'
       OR interaction_status = 'current'
  ) THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION
      'Cannot roll back suggestion constraints while suggestion events remain';
  END IF;

  ALTER TABLE public.events
    DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS events_interaction_type_check,
    ADD CONSTRAINT events_interaction_type_check CHECK (
      interaction_type = ANY (ARRAY['none'::text, 'approval'::text])
    );

  ALTER TABLE public.events
    DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS events_interaction_status_check,
    ADD CONSTRAINT events_interaction_status_check CHECK (
      interaction_status = ANY (ARRAY[
        'pending'::text, 'approved'::text, 'rejected'::text,
        'completed'::text, 'failed'::text
      ])
    );
END
$$;

You're right, and it collapses most of what I proposed.

`events` does carry the interaction (`interaction_type/status/input_schema/input/output/error` + `supersedes_event_id`), and `notification_targets` is exactly a pointer table — the service comment says so itself. And the two-event shape you're describing is **already the established pattern**: `manage_agents.ts:684-745` writes a pending `runs` row, then `insertEvent(… interactionType:'approval', interactionStatus:'pending' …)`, then `notifyActionApprovalNeeded({eventId, runId})` mints the notification pointing at it. `listNotifications` resolves it back through a LEFT JOIN.

So my "new primitive" framing was wrong. There is no new primitive. **The whole queue-an-ask-for-a-human path exists and is ~30 lines; `notifications.send` just isn't allowed to call it.**

## Corrected root cause

Two separate defects, and neither is "missing a card system":

1. **`createNotificationForUsers` hand-rolls its own INSERT into `events`** (service.ts:313) instead of going through `insertEvent`. That's why it drops the card, the interaction columns, and the returned id — it's a drifted second event-writer on the table that already has all of this.
2. **The agent-facing door has a `card` param where it should have had a schema.** `interaction_input_schema` is the ask; `ApproveAction.input` is the answer. A caller-authored `card` with buttons is a category error — presentation carrying routing it can't have.

## Corrected plan

**1. Return the id.** `createNotificationForUsers` → `{created, eventId}`; `handleSend` → `{notified_count, event_id, url}` via `buildResourcePermalink(orgSlug, {kind:'event', eventId})`. One id — `markAsRead` keys on `events.id`, so `notification_id` and `event_id` are the same number and the contract shouldn't invent a distinction. Contract edit ⇒ client-regen gate.

**2. Persist the card as presentation; reject the routing half.** Store `metadata.card`, return it from `listNotifications` + the activity feed (`cardChildToFallbackText` for the text degrade). Reject `actions`/`button` at the `notifications.send` boundary with an error pointing at the schema param. `link-button` stays — it's a URL, it works everywhere.

**3. Let `notifications.send` queue an ask.** One optional `input_schema` param. When present: INSERT a pending `run_type='internal'` run (no connection needed), `insertEvent` with `interactionType:'approval'`, `interactionStatus:'pending'`, `interactionInputSchema`, and point the notification at it — byte-for-byte the `queueWriteForApproval` shape, minus the manage_agents field validation. Register one `BuilderApprovalHandler` whose `apply()` records the human's `input` into `interaction_output` and does nothing else. Returns `run_id` for your `operations.getRun` readback.

Everything else is inherited: human-only gate (agents literally cannot approve), admin-or-owner authority, 7-day expiry (`run_type IN ('action','internal')` is already generic), the append-only supersede chain with reviewer, chat clicks via the existing `run-approval:` prefix, web clicks via the existing `useApproveRun`.

**Net new: one handler entry and one optional field.** No namespace, no table, no migration (`'approval'` is already in the CHECK constraint), no callback bus, no card renderer.

## Three gaps that don't disappear

**Two hardcoded allowlists exclude every non-entity approval — including today's builder approvals.** `buildActionApprovalCard` (triggers.ts:363) returns `undefined` unless `details.kind ∈ {entity_field_change, entity_change}`, so a manage_agents approval gets **no chat buttons at all** right now, just markdown. And `interaction_inline` (activity-feed.ts:340) is an `ENTITY_CHANGE_ACTION_KEYS` membership test, so the inbox shows a review-page CTA instead of inline buttons for the same set. Same shape, same omission, twice. Fix the class: make "renders buttons" / "decidable in place" a property of the registered family instead of two literal lists. That also fixes builder approvals in chat as a side effect.

**The inbox has no input form.** `event-card.tsx:1192-1460` renders `interaction_input_schema` as a real form with input/output/error/reviewer; `attention-inbox.tsx` is a partial reimplementation with Approve/Reject only. So an ask with a schema would show buttons with no fields until the Owletto PR extracts that card and shares it. Either sequence binary asks first, or make the frontend PR a hard prerequisite for shipping `input_schema` — my read is the latter, since shipping a schema nothing renders is the same bug we're fixing.

**Collapsing the duplicate INSERT is not free.** `insertEvent`'s upsert targets `(connection_id, origin_id)`; the notification INSERT upserts on `(organization_id, metadata->>'_lobu_idempotency_key')` and sets no `origin_id` at all. So step 1 adds the columns to the existing INSERT, and the collapse into `insertEvent` is a separate change that has to reconcile the conflict target first. Doing it silently would change idempotency behavior.

---

One thing I still need from you before building step 3, since AGENTS.md says I don't add SDK surface unasked: is `input_schema` on `notifications.send` the field you want, or would you rather the ask be binary-only for v1 (no schema, just Approve/Reject) so the frontend work isn't on the critical path?

**Confidence: high (~90)** on the mechanism — every claim above is read from `origin/main`, and `queueWriteForApproval` is a working template for exactly this. **Medium (~60)** on "builder approvals get no chat buttons today": that's inferred from the `details.kind` early return, not observed on a live Slack card.

**Next actions:**
1. Answer the `input_schema` question — it decides whether the Owletto PR blocks the server PR.
2. Let me ship steps 1+2 now; they're independent of that decision and unblock the id/url half.
3. Live-check the builder-approval chat card (approve-gate a `manage_agents` write against the community Slack bot) to promote that gap to confirmed before I fold it into the class fix.
4. Post the corrected root cause on #2519 so the issue stops describing this as a missing renderer.

Checked — it doesn't. `save_content` (the tool behind `save_memory` and `client.knowledge.save`) takes `entity_ids, content, title, author, semantic_type, payload_type, payload_data, payload_template, attachments, source_url, parent_event_id, idempotency_key, occurred_at, supersedes_event_id, behavior_source`. No recipients, no notify, and no interaction fields either.

And that absence is the root cause one level deeper than where I stopped.

## Why the drift happened

There's one substrate: an `events` row, optionally addressed to users by `notification_targets`. But there are **two doors onto it that each have half the surface**:

| | `save_content` | `notifications.send` |
|---|---|---|
| writes an event | ✅ via `insertEvent` | ✅ via its own hand-rolled INSERT |
| full event surface (attachments, templates, supersedes, entity links) | ✅ | ❌ title + body only |
| interaction columns | ❌ | ❌ |
| addresses it to users | ❌ | ✅ |
| fans out to Slack/Telegram | ❌ | ✅ |

`notifications.send` couldn't reach the addressing primitive from `save_content`, so it grew its own writer — and that writer, being a second copy, never picked up the interaction columns, the card, or the returned id. Every symptom in #2519 falls out of that one split.

So your instinct is right and it's the better fix. The addressing is a property of an event, not a different kind of object.

## What consolidating actually looks like

`createNotificationForUsers` stops hand-rolling its INSERT and calls `insertEvent` — the same writer `save_content` uses. Then a notification is *literally* "an event plus target rows," and everything it was missing arrives at once: the card persists because `metadata` goes through, the id comes back because `insertEvent` returns it, and **`interaction_*` becomes available because it's already a parameter on `insertEvent`** — no new plumbing, no new column, no migration.

`notifications.send` keeps what's genuinely its own: resolving `'admins' | 'all' | [ids]` to user ids, `deliverToBotConnections` (including the preview-mode community-bot branch), the SSE key emit, watcher-reaction tracking. Those are addressing and delivery, which is what it should have been all along.

One real cost I flagged before and it still holds: `insertEvent`'s upsert targets `(connection_id, origin_id)`, while the notification INSERT upserts on `(organization_id, metadata->>'_lobu_idempotency_key')` and sets no `origin_id`. So the collapse has to reconcile the conflict target — it's the one piece of actual work in this, not a mechanical swap.

## What this does to my question

It mostly dissolves it. If the interaction lives on the event — which it does, that's where the column is — then the field belongs on the event-write path, not as a bespoke param on `notifications.send`. Which leaves a cleaner version of the same fork, now about `save_content`:

**Does `save_content` gain the two fields that make an event addressable and answerable** — something like `notify: 'admins' | 'all' | string[]` and `input_schema` — so that "save this, ask these people, read their answer" is one call on one door?

That's a bigger surface change than what I proposed, and it's squarely the kind AGENTS.md says I bring to you first. It's also the one that ends the drift instead of patching around it. The narrower alternative is: collapse the writer now (fixes the card, the id, and unlocks the interaction columns internally), and leave both doors' *public* shapes alone until you've decided whether `save_memory` should be able to page a human.

I'd do the collapse first regardless — it's required for either path and it's where the actual risk is. Want me to scope that as the first PR and hold the surface decision until it's landed?
hmm, how about save_content has a notification flag, or would this make things more complicated?

It makes things *simpler*, but only if you scope it to one of the two things `notifications.send` currently bundles.

## The seam already exists in the code

`createNotificationForUsers` does two separable things, and it already separates them:

```ts
const created = await sql.begin(async (tx) => {
  /* INSERT INTO events … ; INSERT INTO notification_targets … */
});                                    // ← addressing: transactional
if (!created) return { created: false };
deliverToBotConnections(params).catch(…) // ← delivery: fire-and-forget
```

**Addressing** (put this event in these people's inbox) is durable, transactional, cheap, and recoverable — worst case someone marks it read. **Delivery** (push to bound Slack/Telegram channels) is outward-facing, best-effort, and high blast radius.

A flag on `save_content` maps cleanly onto addressing. It maps badly onto delivery — `save_content` is a tool agents call in loops, and a stray flag that posts to everyone's Slack is a spam incident waiting to happen. So:

- `save_content({ …, notify: 'admins' | 'all' | string[] })` → writes the event, addresses it. Inbox only.
- `notifications.send(…)` → the same thing plus `deliverToBotConnections`, i.e. it composes on top rather than running in parallel.

That's not a new concept. It's naming a boundary the code already has.

## Why the flag actually earns its place

This is the part that convinced me it's worth doing rather than just tidy. Compare what each door can write today:

`createNotificationForUsers` hardcodes `payload_type='text'` and `semantic_type='notification'`, and writes only `title`, `payload_text`, `entity_ids`, `client_id`, `metadata`. No attachments. No `payload_template`. No `supersedes_event_id`. No `source_url`.

So right now, if an agent produces something rich — a report with attachments, a JSON-template card, an event that supersedes last week's version — it has to choose between **writing it properly** and **anyone seeing it**. There is no call that does both. That's the real gap, and it's wider than the one #2519 describes.

A `notify` flag on `save_content` closes it in one field, because `save_content` already has the whole event surface. Going the other direction — growing `notifications.send` until it can express attachments and templates — would rebuild `save_content` badly, which is exactly how we got the drifted INSERT in the first place.

## The one honest complication

The inbox has to render arbitrary event types. Today `listNotifications` reads `metadata->>'notification_type'` defaulting to `'generic'`, and `attention-inbox.tsx:106` switches on it (`case "action_approval_needed"` etc.). Events written by `save_content` won't carry a notification type, so they'd all land as `'generic'` — which renders, but as title + body, dropping the attachments and templates that were the point.

That's not a blocker, it's a scoping line: the flag ships useful immediately for text-ish events, and rendering rich payloads in the inbox is a follow-up on the same Owletto card work the interaction form needs anyway. Worth saying out loud rather than discovering it after.

## So, sequencing

1. **Collapse the writer** — `createNotificationForUsers` calls `insertEvent`. Required for any of this, and it's where the actual risk sits (the `(connection_id, origin_id)` vs `_lobu_idempotency_key` conflict-target reconciliation). Fixes the dropped card and the missing id as a side effect.
2. **`notify` flag on `save_content`**, addressing only. Small once step 1 lands, because addressing becomes "insert target rows for an event you already wrote."
3. **Interaction on the event** — falls out for free at that point, since `insertEvent` already takes `interactionType` / `interactionInputSchema`. Whether it's a binary gate or a schema form is then purely a frontend-readiness question, not an API one.

Steps 2 and 3 are both surface changes, so they're yours to approve — but step 1 is unambiguous cleanup that both depend on.

Because interaction columns are **server-minted, never caller-supplied** — and that turns out to be load-bearing.

Every writer that sets `interactionType` in the entire codebase:

```
persist-suggestion.ts:118,309    interactionType: "suggestion"
entity-field-approval.ts:811     interactionType: "approval"
manage_agents.ts:709             interactionType: "approval"
manage_behaviors.ts:740          interactionType: "approval"
manage_operations.ts:1279        interactionType: "approval"
manage_operations.ts:1732        interactionType: "approval"
```

Six call sites, all server-side write gates, and five of the six mint or advance a `runs` row in the same breath. None of them takes the value from a caller. `save_content` doesn't have interactivity for the same reason no agent-facing tool does.

## Why it has to be that way

An interaction isn't a fact — it's a **pending obligation with a state machine living somewhere else**. The event row holds the *description* of the ask; the decidability lives in `runs`: `approval_status` is what `manage_operations approve` claims, what `expire-pending-approvals` sweeps at 7 days, what `requireApprovalAuthority` checks, and what `supersedeActionEvent` keys the audit chain to.

So if `save_content` could just set `interaction_type='approval'`, an agent could write an event that renders as pending with Approve/Reject — backed by no run. The buttons would route to a `run_id` that doesn't exist, the expiry sweep would never see it, and it'd sit "pending" forever. That is *precisely* the #2519 bug, relocated from the card to the column.

The one exception proves it: `persist-suggestion` writes `interaction_type='suggestion'` with no run, and the migration comment spells out why that's safe — suggestions are *"non-blocking: they are never resolved by a click."* Nothing is waiting on them, so there's no state to keep consistent.

## And buttons specifically

Buttons are never caller input anywhere in this system, including the path that works. `buildActionApprovalCard` constructs them server-side:

```ts
Button({ id: `run-approval:${params.runId}:approve`, … })
```

The button id **is** the routing key — `interaction-bridge.ts:901` dispatches on that `run-approval:` prefix. So a button is only meaningful if whoever built it knew a run id, which means only the server can build one. A caller-supplied button is unroutable by construction. That's not a missing feature in `notifications.send`; it's what makes the `card` param a category error.

## What it means for the flag

It rules out the shape that looked simplest. `save_content({ notify, input_schema })` can't be "expose two more columns" — it has to be **"queue an ask,"** which means minting the pending run alongside the event, exactly as `queueWriteForApproval` does at `manage_agents.ts:684-745`.

Which is fine, and it's still one field in the API. But it changes what the field *is*: not a passthrough, a capability. And it means `save_content` grows a second responsibility (creating durable decision state) on top of writing knowledge — which is a real argument for keeping the ask on `notifications.send` after all, where "this needs a human" already fits the tool's job, and leaving `save_content` with just the `notify` addressing flag.

So my read has shifted slightly: **`notify` on `save_content`** (addressing, no state machine, clean), **the ask stays on `notifications.send`** (it mints the run, which is the thing that makes buttons real). Two fields, two doors, each doing the thing that matches its existing job — rather than one door doing both.

Good — that goal changes the answer, and the pieces for it mostly exist already. Here's what I found.

## You already have both halves. They've never met.

**Agents can author templates on the fly today.** `save_content({ payload_type: 'json_template', payload_template })` writes a `JsonTemplate` v1 — data bindings, `if`, `each`, a component set — and `event-card.tsx:2074` renders it with `<JsonRenderer>`. `viewTemplates.set()` does the same for entity tabs, with versioning and rollback.

The renderer is richer than what events get to use:

- **Named actions already exist**: a prop value of `"@approve"` resolves to `context.actions.approve` (renderer.tsx:601). The template names an intent; the *host* supplies the handler. That's the safe shape — same principle as `run-approval:<runId>:approve`, minus the encoding.
- **App components already exist**: `entity-table`, `entity-board`, `metric-series`, `entity-link` via `RenderContext.components`. `entity-board` even takes `onUpdate(entityId, patch)` — a real write-back.
- **But event templates get neither.** `event-card.tsx:2080` calls `<JsonRenderer template data />` and passes no `actions`, no `components`. So an agent-authored event template today is display-only by omission, not by design.

And the DSL has **no input components at all** — `ComponentType` is card/badge/button/alert/table/text. `button` renders, but there's nothing to type into and nothing to submit.

Meanwhile the *other* half — `interaction_input_schema` + `approve({ run_id, input })` — has real inputs, server-side validation, durable pending state, expiry, authz, and a typed readback. But zero layout control: you get whatever form the schema implies.

**Templates have layout and no return path. Interactions have a return path and no layout.**

## The design

Don't pick one. Bind them, because they're answering different questions:

- **`interaction_input_schema` = what is being asked.** Field names, types, enums, required. The server validates against it, the agent reads typed values back out of `interaction_output`, and chat can mechanically derive a card from it. This is the contract.
- **`payload_template` = how it looks.** Optional. Agent-authored, arbitrary layout, full DSL. Web renders it. Omit it and you get the auto-generated form `event-card.tsx` already builds today.

The binding is one new component type:

```json
{ "type": "field", "props": { "name": "tone" } }
```

The renderer looks `tone` up in the event's `interaction_input_schema`, picks the control from its type/enum, and writes into the same `formValues` state that `approve({ run_id, input: formValues })` already submits. Submit itself is the existing `@action` mechanism — the host binds `approve`/`reject` into `context.actions` for interaction-bearing events, and the template references them by name.

So the agent writes a real template with a real form, and we add **one component type and one context wiring** — not a form framework. Validation, types, and required-ness stay in JSON Schema where they already are, and stay enforced server-side where an agent-authored value can't bypass them.

## What's new vs. reused

| | |
|---|---|
| Template DSL, bindings, loops, conditionals | reused |
| `@action` name→handler binding | reused |
| App component registry | reused |
| JSON-Schema form controls + `formValues` | reused (`event-card.tsx:1192-1460`) |
| `approve({run_id, input})` submit + validation | reused |
| Durable pending state, 7d expiry, human-only gate, audit chain | reused |
| **`field` component type** | new, small |
| **Pass `actions` + `components` to event templates** | new, one call site |
| **Server: let an agent queue an ask (schema + optional template), minting the run** | new, ~30 lines, copies `queueWriteForApproval` |

## What genuinely doesn't exist yet

**Chat can't render this.** `JsonTemplate` is web-only. The `chat` package does have `TextInput`/`Select`/`Modal` and `actionType:"modal"`, but `interaction-bridge.ts` has **no modal-submit handler at all** — I grepped, there's no branch. So phase one: web gets the template form, chat gets a schema-derived card for simple asks and a "Review in Lobu" link for anything with fields. Deriving Block Kit from the schema is tractable later precisely *because* the schema is the contract; it would be impossible from an arbitrary layout template.

**Agent-authored templates would render in an admin's inbox.** The renderer is a closed component set rather than raw HTML, which is the right starting point, but I haven't checked what the `markdown` component sanitizes or whether the `redactBodyUrls` treatment the activity feed applies to notification bodies covers template content. Worth verifying before this renders anywhere privileged — not a blocker, but not something to discover afterward.

## Sequencing

1. **Collapse the notification writer into `insertEvent`.** Everything else needs it, and it's where the real risk is (the conflict-target reconciliation). Fixes the dropped card and the missing id on the way past.
2. **Pass `actions` + `components` to event templates.** Independent, small, and immediately makes agent-authored event templates first-class instead of accidentally crippled.
3. **`field` component + host-bound `@approve`/`@reject`.** Owletto PR, needs `make ui-review`.
4. **Server-side "queue an ask"** carrying schema + optional template.
5. **Chat modal path**, if and when it's worth it.

Steps 2 and 3 are the ones that deliver what you actually asked for; 1 is the prerequisite; 4 is what makes it reachable from an agent.

The one thing I'd still want your call on: whether the schema stays **required** for an interactive template. I'd keep it required — it's what makes the answer typed, server-validatable, and chat-renderable, and without it `interaction_input` becomes an untrusted free-form blob from a worker the codebase elsewhere explicitly treats as untrusted. But it does mean an agent authoring a form writes two things, and if you'd rather it write one, that's a real trade and it's yours.

Yes and no, and the distinction changes the design — enough that I'd drop the `field`-component idea I proposed last turn.

## What the Chat SDK actually ships

I read `node_modules/chat/dist/index.d.ts`. Converters exported: `toSlack`, `toDiscord`, `toGChat`, `toMarkdown`, `toPlainText`, `toJSON`, `toAst`, `tableToAscii`, plus `fromSlack` / `fromTeams` / `fromGChat` / `fromJSON` / `fromReactElement`.

**There is no `toReact` / `toHtml` / `toDom`.** The package has no `react` dependency at all — `fromReactElement` runs the other direction (JSX → CardElement). And owletto has zero `CardElement` references anywhere in `src`. So for the browser, the renderer doesn't exist and never did.

But look at what it *does* have that we've been talking about building:

```
Modal, ModalElement, toModalElement, ModalSubmitEvent, ModalSubmitHandler,
TextInput, Select, SelectOption, RadioSelect, ActionEvent, ActionHandler
```

A complete form system with a typed submit event, already serializing to every chat platform. That's the thing I was about to reinvent as a `field` component on `JsonTemplate`.

One caveat you should weigh: **none of it is used anywhere in this repo.** I grepped `packages/server` and `packages/connectors` for `TextInput` / `Select` / `RadioSelect` / `Modal` / `ModalSubmit` — zero hits outside an unrelated Bedrock helper. The Chat SDK's form capability is entirely unexercised here, and `interaction-bridge.ts` has no modal-submit branch. So it's a real path, not a proven one.

## What that changes

My last proposal was wrong in shape: extending `JsonTemplate` with inputs gives you a form that works on **one** surface, and then you still build the chat modal path separately. Using CardElement gives you a form that works on **all** of them, and the only missing renderer is the web one.

So: **CardElement is the DSL for asks.** Author it (the agent can even write JSX), `toSlack`/`toDiscord`/`toGChat` handle chat for free, and owletto gets one new renderer — roughly the size of the `json-renderer` it already has.

This does *not* subsume `JsonTemplate`, and they shouldn't be merged. Different jobs:

| | CardElement | JsonTemplate |
|---|---|---|
| shape | message / form | data view |
| surfaces | chat + web | web |
| has | inputs, modals, typed submit | `if`/`each`, data bindings, `entity-table`/`entity-board`/`metric-series` |
| use for | an ask that must reach someone wherever they are | a rich agent-authored view in the app |

Splitting by *job* rather than by surface is what keeps both coherent. Trying to make one serve both is how you get a third half-system.

## It also answers the question I left open

Last turn I asked whether the agent has to author both a schema and a template. With CardElement, no — **the card is the schema.** Its `TextInput`/`Select`/`RadioSelect` children declare the field names and allowed values structurally, so the server can derive `interaction_input_schema` from the card at queue time. That keeps `approve({ run_id, input })` validating exactly as it does today, keeps `event-card.tsx`'s existing schema-driven form working as the fallback when there's no card, and the agent writes one thing.

## What's actually left to build

1. **Collapse the notification writer into `insertEvent`** — unchanged prerequisite, still where the real risk sits.
2. **CardElement → React renderer in owletto.** The one substantial new piece. Owletto PR, `make ui-review`.
3. **Server: queue an ask.** Persist the card, derive `interaction_input_schema` from its inputs, mint the pending run. ~30 lines on the `queueWriteForApproval` template.
4. **Web submit** → the existing `approve({ run_id, input })`. No new endpoint.
5. **Chat modal-submit branch** in `interaction-bridge.ts` → the same `approve`. This is the piece I'd probe first, since nothing in this codebase has ever exercised `toSlack` on a `Modal`.

`JsonTemplate` stays where it is for data views — and separately, passing `actions` + `components` into `event-card.tsx:2080`'s `<JsonRenderer>` is still worth doing on its own, since agent-authored event templates are display-only today by omission rather than intent.

Before committing to any of this I'd spend one session on step 5's probe — post a `Modal` card to the community Slack bot and see whether `toSlack` produces a valid view and whether a submit event even reaches us. If that path is broken upstream, the design holds but the sequencing changes: web-first, chat later.

Honest answer: no, and the reason they're separate is historical, not architectural.

## Why they're separate

`chat` is **vendored** — `"chat": "^4.26.0"` in `packages/server/package.json`, with `@workflow/serde`, `remark`, `unified` underneath it. It's Vercel's Chat SDK. Lobu didn't design that DSL; its shape is the lowest common denominator of Block Kit / Adaptive Cards / Discord / Google Chat, and it's on someone else's release cycle.

`JsonTemplate` is **homegrown** — Lobu's own SPA view DSL, built for entity tabs, with data bindings, `if`/`each`, and app components like `entity-board`.

Two DSLs because one arrived with the chat integration and one was written for the web app. Neither was designed against the other. That's all.

## But merging them is the wrong fix

CardElement's ceiling is permanently set by Slack — it can never carry `entity-board` or a SQL-bound table. JsonTemplate can never render in a Slack thread. Merging means either bloating one with things half its targets can't draw, or forking a vendored dependency. Both bad.

The actual mistake is upstream of the DSL question, and I walked past it for two turns: **presentation shouldn't be the agent's contract at all.**

## The layering

- **Layer 1 — the ask.** What's being requested, what shape the answer takes. `interaction_input_schema` + the durable run. Platform-independent, validatable, typed.
- **Layer 2 — presentation.** Derived from layer 1 by default. Overridable per-surface when an agent genuinely cares: CardElement for message-shaped surfaces, JsonTemplate for app surfaces.
- **Layer 3 — transport.** Chat adapters, SSE, inbox.

Under that, plural layer-2 renderers are fine — surfaces really do differ, and a renderer per surface family is normal. What's broken today is that **layer 1 isn't exposed to agents at all.** The only thing `notifications.send` accepts is a card, so the agent is forced to author presentation, and then that presentation carries routing it structurally cannot have. That *is* #2519. Not a missing renderer — a missing contract.

The database already agrees with this, by the way: `interaction_input_schema`, `interaction_input`, `interaction_output` are columns. The card is not a column. The schema models intent; presentation was always meant to be derived. `cardChildToFallbackText` exists precisely because presentation has to degrade.

## The test that settles it

What happens when a fourth surface shows up — email digest, mobile push, an MCP client, voice?

If the **card is the contract**, every new surface needs its own CardElement renderer or it gets nothing, and voice gets nothing forever because you cannot speak a Block Kit view.

If the **schema is the contract**, every surface renders it in its own idiom. Voice asks "formal or warm?" out loud. Email renders radio buttons. MCP returns a tool result the client renders however it likes. And the card, where one exists, is a bonus skin for the surfaces that can use it.

That's the long-term architecture. Two renderers isn't the problem; a missing contract above them is.

## What it changes in the plan

This is a real revision of what I said the last two turns — I had CardElement as "the DSL for asks." It shouldn't be. The schema is the ask; the card is an optional override.

And that makes the whole thing *cheaper*, because both default renderers already exist:

- **schema → web form**: `event-card.tsx:1192-1460`, already built, already wired to `approve({ run_id, input })`
- **schema → chat buttons**: `buildActionApprovalCard`, already built, already routed by the `run-approval:` prefix

So the shippable core needs **no new renderer at all**:

1. Collapse the notification writer into `insertEvent` — still the prerequisite, still where the risk is.
2. Let an agent queue an ask: `input_schema` + the pending run. This is now the center of the work, not a step in it.
3. Widen the two allowlists (`buildActionApprovalCard`'s `details.kind` gate, `interaction_inline`'s `ENTITY_CHANGE_ACTION_KEYS`) so a family declares its own renderability instead of being hardcoded — which also fixes builder approvals getting no chat buttons today.
4. Share the form-capable card into the attention inbox, replacing its thinner reimplementation.

Everything I raised last turn — the CardElement→React renderer, the chat modal-submit branch, the Slack `Modal` probe — moves to **optional layer-2 overrides**, deferred until an agent actually needs a layout the schema can't express. Which may be never.

So the answer to "is this the best long-term architecture": the two DSLs are fine and should stay. What needs building is the layer above them, and it turns out to be the smallest version of this work, not the largest.

content.text:
Let me trace it literally, because the answer today is unsatisfying in an informative way.

## Today

You ask me. I call, via `run_sdk`:

```ts
await client.notifications.send({
  title: 'Which tone for the Acme follow-up?',
  body: 'Formal or warm?',
  recipients: [<your user id>],
});
```

What runs:

1. `notify.handleSend` resolves `recipients` → user ids.
2. `createNotificationForUsers` opens a transaction: `INSERT INTO events` (`semantic_type='notification'`, title, `payload_text` = body, `metadata.notification_type='agent_message'`) then `INSERT INTO notification_targets (event_id, user_id)`.
3. `emit(orgId, { keys: ['notifications', 'notifications-unread-count'] })` → your open tab's SSE invalidates those query keys → the inbox refetches.
4. Fire-and-forget `deliverToBotConnections` — no-op if you have no bound Slack/Telegram channel.
5. Returns `{ notified_count: 1 }`.

What you see: a row in the attention inbox. Title, body, unread dot. **That's the whole thing.** No buttons, no field, nothing to answer with.

What I get back: `{ notified_count: 1 }`. Not the id, not a URL. If you then asked "where'd it go?", I'd have to call `notifications.list` and match on the title.

If I tried to attach buttons via the `card` param, the card is discarded at step 2 — `service.ts:313` writes only title, `payload_text`, and `metadata`, so the web literally never receives it. On Slack it would *render*, and clicking would fall through `registerActionHandlers`' prefix set into a silent no-op.

So to actually get your answer today, my only working option is to ask you **in chat** — where `postQuestion` → SSE → `interaction-card.tsx` renders a real question card with option buttons that route back. But that's conversation-scoped, needs a live session, and isn't a notification.

**Lobu can ask you a question in a chat thread today. It cannot ask you a question in your inbox.** That's the whole of #2519 in one sentence.

## Under the design

```ts
const { run_id, url } = await client.notifications.send({
  title: 'Which tone for the Acme follow-up?',
  recipients: [<your user id>],
  input_schema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: { tone: { type: 'string', enum: ['formal', 'warm'] } },
    required: ['tone'],
  },
});
```

1. Server mints a pending `runs` row (`run_type='internal'`, no connection) and an event with `interaction_type='approval'`, `interaction_status='pending'`, `interaction_input_schema` = that schema.
2. The notification points at it — same `resource_type='event'` / `resource_id` shape every built-in approval already uses.
3. `listNotifications`' existing LEFT JOIN resolves the pending run, so the inbox row comes back already knowing it's actionable.
4. You see the ask **with a tone selector and a confirm button**, rendered by the same schema-driven form `event-card.tsx:1192-1460` already draws for connector approvals.
5. You pick "warm" and confirm → `approve({ run_id, input: { tone: 'warm' } })` → validated against the schema, `interaction_output` written, the event superseded to `approved` with you stamped as reviewer.
6. I poll `operations.getRun({ run_id })` and read `interaction_output.tone` — typed, not parsed out of a message.

If you also had Slack bound, the same ask arrives there as buttons via the existing `run-approval:` routing, and whichever surface you answer on resolves the other — because both are decisions on one run, not two copies of a message.

And I can tell you where it landed, because `url` came back from the call.

## Why I'm confident this is the right shape

I found a fourth view DSL while checking this: `interaction-card.tsx` in owletto defines `InteractionView` / `InteractionBlock` — `text | code | entity | diff` blocks plus actions, with the comment *"Adding an interaction type is a new view."* The SPA builds that view client-side from a semantic payload the server sends.

So the count is four presentation DSLs — `chat` CardElement, `JsonTemplate`, `InteractionView`, and schema-driven forms. Under "pick one DSL," that's a mess. Under the layering, it's just four surfaces each rendering the same intent their own way — **and the conversation path already works exactly that way.** The server sends what's being asked; the client decides how it looks.

The notification path is the one that never got wired to it. That's not a new architecture I'm proposing; it's the pattern already in the codebase, applied to the door that missed it.

**Confidence: high (~90)** on the today-path trace — every step read from `origin/main`. **Medium (~70)** on the `InteractionView` characterization: I read the type and the card component, but its builder is host-injected through a provider and I didn't trace where the mapping actually happens.

**Next actions:**
1. Let me ship the writer collapse + id/url return — it's a prerequisite for all of this and independently fixes "I can't tell you where it landed."
2. Post the corrected root cause on #2519, since the issue still frames this as a missing card renderer.
3. If you want the walkthrough proven rather than described, I can send you a real notification on prod right now and we'd both see exactly the dead-end above.
